column4: Sacrificial camels stand صَوَافَّ in rows, God’s name is spoken over them, then their meat feeds both the contented القانع and the asker; this gathers the section’s camel, صفّ, remembrance, sufficiency, food, and subjection in one scene.
Pure, easy-swallowed milk is given from inside livestock between waste and blood; it directly realizes the section’s udder, milk, watering, and ساغ detail.
The hell-dweller gulps the drink ولا يكاد يسيغه, the exact reversal of the livestock milk that is سَائِغًا in 16:66 and of the section’s nourishing camel drink.
God creates livestock for warmth, benefits, and food, directly presenting the camel as a created, many-sided human provision.
Livestock are beautiful when brought home in the evening and driven to pasture in the morning; that daily herd rhythm makes concrete the section’s day-long camel travel and return at night.
Livestock carry human loads to a country people could scarcely reach unaided, directly matching the camel as mount, bearer, and means of distant travel.
God asks whether people see that His hands’ work, عملت أيدينا, created livestock for them; this directly answers the section’s working-camel sense of ع م ل by relocating the decisive work to God.
God makes the livestock tractable, ذللناها, so people ride and eat; the same lowering that can mark humiliation becomes mercy when applied to the camel.
Livestock skins become portable houses and their wool, fur, and hair become furnishings and goods, exactly the section’s claim that the camel furnishes the room around its rider.
Lean mounts come from every deep pass to the pilgrimage; their يأتين joins the source section’s gait sense under أ ت ي with the camel’s long-distance journey.
The command that the human look at his food repeats the section’s commanded gaze at the camel while redirecting sight toward the provision the animal also supplies.
Fruit and pasture are the last named growth in the food sequence; the pasture specifically prepares 80:32’s provision for livestock and the camel that lives from fresh herbage.
The whole food scene is declared a provision for people and their livestock, explicitly completing the gaze begun at 80:24 with the human-animal pair developed in the section.
Water descends for human drink and grows vegetation in which animals graze, directly joining the section’s water, fresh pasture, and camel subsistence.
Livestock provide milk from their bellies, many other benefits, and food, concentrating the same animal body and human uses traced through the section.
People are carried on livestock and ships; after 23:21’s milk and food, this adds the camel’s transport function.
Livestock give further benefits and drinks, completing 36:71–72’s creation, riding, and eating with the section’s milk-bearing animal.
God makes livestock so that people may ride some and eat some, a direct summary of the camel’s two central uses in the section.
Livestock meet needs held in human breasts and carry people as ships do, extending 40:79 from food and riding to purposeful travel.
God creates the pairs and provides ships and livestock as mounts, locating camel travel within the ordered gift of creation.
The rider settles on the mount’s back and remembers the One who subjected it; this is the section’s striking relation that the camel is beside the human while the human is upon it.
The mount prayer ends by declaring return to the Lord, joining the section’s camel journey and nightly return to the surah’s final return to God.
God makes the earth tractable, tells people to walk its paths and eat His provision, and ends with resurrection to Him; it parallels the tractable camel’s route, food, and ultimate return.
Livestock include load-bearing animals and animals kept close to the ground, and people may eat God’s provision; this directly frames the camel as burden bearer and food.
The camel pair is named explicitly while false claims about males, females, and womb contents are challenged, adding sex and reproduction to the image of the created camel body.
Salih presents God’s she-camel as a sign, tells his people to let her graze in God’s land, and forbids harm; camel, pasture, creation-sign, and human responsibility all meet.
The she-camel is God’s sign and must be left to feed in His land, directly repeating the camel-at-pasture scene and its protected status.
The she-camel receives an allotted turn to drink and the people theirs, a precise boundary around س ق ي that counters the section’s camel able to subsist on moist pasture.
God sends the she-camel as a trial and commands watchful patience, making the animal itself a divine sign at which humans must learn how to look.
Water is divided and every drinking turn attended, supplying the concrete watering rule for the she-camel introduced in 54:27.
God’s messenger warns the people to respect God’s she-camel and her drink, again binding the camel sign to a protected share of water.
At the final upheaval even pregnant she-camels, prized living wealth, are abandoned; this sharply confirms the section’s camel-as-fortune while showing fortune’s limit.
Hell’s sparks are likened to yellow camels, bringing the section’s familiar animal into the fire scene that precedes its command to look.
A camel cannot pass through a needle’s eye, and that bodily scale marks the barred entry to heaven; the animal invited as a visible sign in the section becomes a measure of impossibility.
The condemned drink like desperately thirsty camels, reversing the section’s camel that can make do with moist pasture and completing 56:52–54’s hell food-and-drink scene.
The brothers expect an added camel-load of grain, so the camel’s carrying capacity becomes a unit of measured provision and family subsistence.
A drinking cup is placed in a saddlebag before the caravan is hailed; cup, baggage, provisioning, and camel travel meet just as milk cups and journey meet in the section.
The lost drinking cup is paired with a camel-load as reward, again joining vessel, load, value, and caravan economy in one ayah.
Pilgrims mention God over sacrificial livestock, eat from them, and feed the destitute, anticipating the lined camel and feeding instructions of 22:36.
Sacrificial animals provide benefits until their appointed term and destination at the Ancient House, joining useful livestock with pilgrimage and eventual slaughter.
Every community receives a rite in which God’s name is mentioned over the livestock He provides, setting the broader rule behind the section’s sacrificial camels.
Neither the animals’ meat nor blood reaches God; piety does, and their subjection should produce magnification and gratitude, defining the spiritual boundary of the camel sacrifice in 22:36.
Paradise contains rivers of milk whose taste never changes, extending the section’s pure animal milk and prepared cups into an unspoiled heavenly provision.

The verse details a restriction on cattle and sheep fat, except what clings to backs, entrails, or bones; it directly illuminates the section’s س م ن branch, marrow fat, and edible animal body through a legal boundary.
Abraham brings his guests a fat calf; the livestock’s fatness, under the section’s س م ن branch, becomes food and hospitality.
Thirst, fatigue نَصَب, and hunger incurred on a journey in God’s path form the same bodily triad as the section’s water-saving, feeding, day-traveling camel.
Moses’ companion says that their journey has brought fatigue نَصَبًا, the direct travel sense activated by the section’s ن ص ب dictionary branch.
People are told to eat and pasture their livestock among the plants God brings forth, directly staging shared human and animal provision.
Rain revives dead land and gives drink to many livestock and people, linking divine watering to the herd’s life rather than treating water as an isolated substance.
People are asked whether they see water driven to barren land and crops eaten by both their livestock and themselves, closely matching the section’s look at camel and food.
From the spread earth God brings out its water and pasture, the two resources whose unusual relation defines the camel in the section.
Water, pasture, and the ordered earth are declared provision for people and livestock, completing 79:31 in the same human-animal pairing as 80:32.
God brings out fresh pasture, the very food by which the source section says the camel can dispense with direct water for a time.
Livestock are listed among the adorned stores of worldly wealth, directly supporting the section’s Arabic picture of the camel as property and fortune.
Livestock and children are named as reinforcements of worldly abundance, confirming the herd as a visible form of wealth and divine provision.
The eight livestock pairs and their formation in wombs place sex, gestation, and animal creation behind the section’s milk-bearing female camel.
The people hamstring the she-camel and defy their Lord’s command, reversing 7:73’s required gaze, grazing freedom, and care into destruction.
After the she-camel is hamstrung, only three days remain before punishment; the killed sign turns the useful protected animal into the boundary of judgment.
Salih forbids touching the she-camel with harm and ties violation to a tremendous day, stating the moral boundary around 26:155’s shared water.
They hamstring the she-camel and become regretful, the direct reversal of allowing the animal its measured drink.
The people summon their companion, who seizes and hamstrings the she-camel, turning the watched trial of 54:27 into deliberate violence.
They deny the messenger and hamstring the she-camel, so destruction follows; the creature whose drink was protected in 91:13 becomes the test they fail.
Fresh pasture becomes dark stubble, setting the camel’s moist sustaining herbage against the same vegetation after it has lost its nourishment.
Satan’s program includes slitting livestock ears and altering God’s creation, the human mutilation of animals set against looking rightly at how the camel was created.
Invented rules bar access to certain livestock backs and foods, reversing the divinely given riding and eating uses developed throughout the section.
People falsely reserve what is in livestock wombs for men and exclude women, imposing a human food boundary on the animal body that God provides.
Consecrated animal categories are rejected as human inventions; the verse checks attempts to remove valuable animals, especially camel categories, from their God-given uses.
Sacrificial animals are detained from reaching their appointed place at Hudaybiyya, a historical interruption of the pilgrimage movement and slaughter completed in 22:33–36.
Rain-fed growth eaten by people and livestock suddenly becomes reaped debris, showing the transience of the pasture on which the camel’s sufficiency depends.
Seven lean cows consume seven fat cows, using animal fatness as the visible boundary between abundance and famine beside the section’s fat, food, and livestock wealth.
The commanded cow is specifically one not trained to plow or water a field, the opposite of the source section’s yaʿmala, a female camel naturally fitted for work.
A donkey bearing books provides a negative image of animal load-bearing: physical carriage remains while human understanding fails, unlike the camel’s load as an intelligible blessing.
No morally burdened soul can make another carry its load, whereas the camel mercifully carries loads people could not transport themselves; literal service marks the limit of moral transfer.
God removes the Prophet’s burden, using the source section’s و ض ع root in a figurative unloading that 94:3 locates on the back.
The burden had weighed upon the back, making 94:2’s relief a pointed human counterpart to the camel carrying another’s heavy load.
Panting mounts charge at speed, a sharp gait contrast to the source section’s gentle all-day camel walk and its lexicon of faster and slower steps.

The wrongdoers eat from the tree of Zaqqum; this hell plant is a dark counterpart to the source dictionary’s pasture plant called “camel bread” and begins the scene ending with thirsty camels in 56:55.
They fill their bellies from Zaqqum, turning a plant into compulsory excess rather than the camel’s modest sufficiency; 56:55 supplies the camel comparison.
Boiling water follows the hell food, joining eating and forced drinking before 56:55 likens the drinkers to thirsty camels.
Huge sparks are thrown from the fire; this ayah supplies the object whose shape or movement 77:33 compares with yellow camels.
Poured water is the first material step in the food chain opened at 80:24 and completed as provision for livestock at 80:32.
The earth is split open so growth can emerge, preparing the pasture and animal provision named later in 80:31–32.
Grain is one product of the opened earth in the inspected food scene whose conclusion includes livestock.
Grapes and green fodder are brought forth; the vegetation gives concrete content to the camel’s fresh-herbage diet before 80:32 names livestock.
Olives and palms add human food to the same created provision that culminates in shared human and livestock benefit.
Dense gardens locate the growing environment from which 80:31’s fruit and pasture emerge for the two beneficiaries of 80:32.
God makes paths through the earth and sends water that produces paired plants, joining the camel journey’s route to the pasture eaten in 20:54.

The humbled earth خَاشِعَةً stirs and swells after rain; the source section’s خ ش ع branch describes an exhausted camel hump sinking, while this use leads back to the rain-fed pasture that restores animal life.
A mountain would become humbled and split from fear of God; it transfers the source section’s خ ش ع image of a collapsed camel hump to the distant high object set beside the camel in surah 88.
God creates every animal from water and includes those walking on four legs; the camel belongs to that created class even though the section stresses its unusual ability to delay drinking.
Livestock vary in color alongside people and other creatures, supplying another visible feature through which an observer can recognize deliberate animal creation.
God makes livestock in pairs and multiplies them, giving the reproductive basis of the herds treated as wealth and milk-bearing provision in the section.
Horses, mules, and donkeys are named for riding and adornment after the load-bearing livestock, defining the camel’s place among other mounts by comparison.
Grazing livestock are made lawful as food while pilgrimage hunting has a limit, framing animal use as granted rather than simply possessed.
Sacrificial animals and their garlands must not be violated, protecting the pilgrimage herd before the lined slaughter described in 22:36.
A pilgrim who kills game owes an equivalent from livestock as an offering reaching the Kaaba, placing animal value, sacrifice, and pilgrimage under a measured legal boundary.
The pilgrim must send an available sacrificial animal and wait until it reaches its place, an earlier formulation of the camel offering’s journey and appointed slaughter.
The pilgrimage passage commands taking provision while calling piety the best provision, adding the inward measure to 2:196’s animal offering and travel.
A caravan sends its water-drawer and a bucket brings Joseph up, pairing desert travel with the act of drawing water that also governs the camel’s life.
Moses beats down leaves with his staff for his sheep, a concrete herdsman action that parallels managing a camel herd’s access to forage.
At Midian shepherds water their flocks while two women hold theirs back, staging herd, herder, and scarce shared water around the same س ق ي relation as the camel passages.
Moses waters the women’s animals, supplying the act withheld in 28:23 and turning access to water into care for a herd.
Sheep graze through a cultivated field by night, showing that pasturing a herd also requires custody and boundaries, not merely available vegetation.
One ewe versus ninety-nine makes herd size a form of property and power, a smaller-animal parallel to the camel wealth named in the section.
Abraham brings a roasted calf to his guests, another livestock body turned into generous food beside the section’s marrow, fat, and meat senses.
The community had urged neither horses nor riding camels toward the recovered property, so the exact camel mount appears through the absence of a journey or charge.
Quraysh’s winter and summer caravan journeys provide the social and economic setting in which camel travel, nightly stopping, and animal wealth belong together.
Human beings are carried on land and sea and given good provisions; the land half is realized concretely by the burden-bearing mounts paired with ships elsewhere.

The Event is “lowering, raising,” a judgment-day pairing that echoes the source section’s opposed raised and lowered camel gaits while distinguishing those side senses from the ayah’s cosmic reversal.
God raises the sky and sets down the balance, placing the section’s ر ف ع and و ض ع opposition in a cosmic ordering rather than an animal gait.

Mountains are commanded to echo or return with David under the أ و ب root; the source section uses that root for the camel’s day journey and evening return, so even the distant mountain participates in responsive return.
The birds are gathered and each is أَوَّاب, turning the source section’s return-at-night root into a collected creaturely return rather than a camel caravan.
The lasting abode is a place where no fatigue نَصَب touches its people, the restful endpoint that answers the source section’s all-day journey and 18:62’s travel weariness.
No fatigue touches the people of the garden and they will not be expelled, opposing the tiring movement and temporary night stop contained in the section’s camel vocabulary.
People divide crops and livestock between God and their partners, corrupting the camel herd’s status as a whole gift and form of wealth.
Those who forbid God’s livestock provision through fabrication are declared lost, closing the false-use sequence that 6:138–139 specifies.
Zaqqum is a tree growing in the root of Hell, a fire-grown plant that reverses the source dictionary’s ordinary fodder plant called “camel bread.”
The condemned eat from Zaqqum and fill their bellies, a punitive plant meal opposed to the little fresh forage that suffices the camel.
People are commanded to look at fruit when it forms and ripens, another disciplined gaze at created food that can train the look directed at camel and provision.
The command وانحر plausibly evokes animal sacrifice, traditionally including the camel slaughter enacted explicitly in 22:36, though this ayah itself does not name the animal.
